theorem.statement:
Suppose the fixed-design, fixed-exposure, imputability, and fixed-rank-statistic premises hold, and suppose \(K\) is row-stochastic, outcome-free, and satisfies \(d_K(A)\geq\pi(A)\) for every nonempty \(A\subseteq\Omega\).  
The weak-order handle has an exact finite reduction and its inversion is simultaneously valid, but the full positive answer requested in the question is false for the frozen schedule-score definition.  More precisely, fix the realized assignment \(x_0\in\Omega\).  Enumerate a binary vector \(b\in\{0,1\}^{U}\) with \(\sum_{u\in U}b_u\leq r\) and, for every \(x\in\Omega\), a weak order \(\omega_x\) of the \(N\) values \(\{v_{u,Z_u(x)}:u\in U\}\), where \(v_{ua}\) denotes \(\theta_u(a,e)\).  Let \(\mathcal F_{b,\boldsymbol\omega}(x_0,c)\) be the set of \(v\in\mathbb R^{U\times\{0,1\}}\) satisfying
\[
 v_{u,Z_u(x_0)}=Y^{\mathrm{obs}}_u,\qquad
 b_u=1\Longleftrightarrow v_{u1}-v_{u0}>c,
\]
and all equality and strict-order relations specified by the weak orders \(\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_x:x\in\Omega)\).  If \(q_x(\omega_x)\) is the value of the fixed rank statistic \(T\) on that weak-order cell, then
\[
 p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{r,c}(x_0)
 =
 \max_{\substack{b,\boldsymbol\omega:\;\sum_u b_u\leq r\\
                   \mathcal F_{b,\boldsymbol\omega}(x_0,c)\neq\varnothing}}
 \sum_{y\in\Omega}K(x_0,y)
 \mathbf 1\!\left\{q_y(\omega_y)\geq q_{x_0}(\omega_{x_0})\right\}.
\]
Every cell-feasibility question is an exact finite linear feasibility problem with weak and strict affine inequalities; equivalently, it is decided by a max-slack linear program or by finite Fourier--Motzkin elimination with strictness flags.  Thus at most \(2^N |\mathfrak W_N|^m\) cells, where \(\mathfrak W_N\) is the finite set of weak orders on \(N\) labeled elements, compute the value and return an optimizing compatible schedule.  Treating \(c\) as one more scalar variable gives a terminating exact parametric version for inversion.  In particular, this formulation solves the three-assignment, two-unit coupled pattern.

For every \(1\leq k\leq N\), with the extended-real convention \(\sup\varnothing=-\infty\), the projection has the explicit nested-test form
\[
 \ell_k(e;\alpha)
 =\sup\left\{c\in\mathbb R:
 p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{N-k,c}(X)\leq\alpha\right\},
\]
and
\[
 \Pr_{X\sim\pi}\!\left\{
 \tau_{(k)}(e)\geq\ell_k(e;\alpha)
 \text{ for every }k=1,\ldots,N
 \right\}\geq 1-\alpha.
\]
Nevertheless, the demanded exact recovery of the two advertised no-interference comparator reductions fails.  In the two-unit, one-treated complete-randomization cell with uniform \(\pi\), uniform partition kernel \(K\), \(\phi(j)=j\), and schedule
\[
 \theta_1(0,e)=1,\quad \theta_1(1,e)=3,
 \qquad
 \theta_2(0,e)=0,\quad \theta_2(1,e)=2,
\]
the frozen score map at the assignment treating unit \(1\) gives \(p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{0,2}=1\), whereas the fixed adjusted-outcome rank reduction gives \(1/2\).  The one-stratum Su--Li case contains the same witness.  Hence the exact finite network computation and simultaneous projection are positive, but they are not a strict extension of those comparator reductions under the frozen definition \(s_\theta(x)=T(x,Y_\theta(x))\).
theorem.proof_tex:
Fix a realization \(X=x_0\).  We first prove the finite reduction.  By \(\texttt{ass:fixed-peer-exposure}\), every focal unit has peer exposure \(e\) at every assignment in \(\Omega\).  Therefore the only coordinates of a candidate schedule that can enter a score are
\[
 v_{ua}:=\theta_u(a,e),\qquad u\in U,\quad a\in\{0,1\},
\]
and schedule consistency gives
\[
 Y_\theta(x)_u=v_{u,Z_u(x)}
 \quad(x\in\Omega,u\in U),
 \qquad
 v_{u,Z_u(x_0)}=Y^{\mathrm{obs}}_u.
 \tag{1}
\]
The first identity uses the potential-outcome interpretation of \(Y_\theta\) in \(\texttt{def:schedule-score}\); the second is precisely the observed-data consistency clause in \(\texttt{def:bounded-null-schedules}\).  Coordinates of \(\theta\) at exposures other than \(e\) may be chosen arbitrarily after \(v\) is fixed, because they enter neither (1) nor the effect-count restriction.  Thus restriction to \(v\) loses no compatible schedule, and every feasible \(v\) extends to one.

For each \(u\), define
\[
 b_u(v,c):=\mathbf 1\{v_{u1}-v_{u0}>c\}.
 \tag{2}
\]
The bounded-null condition in \(\texttt{def:bounded-null-schedules}\) is exactly
\[
 \sum_{u\in U}b_u(v,c)\leq r.
 \tag{3}
\]
For a fixed binary pattern \(b\), (2) is represented without relaxation by
\[
 \begin{cases}
 v_{u1}-v_{u0}>c,&b_u=1,\\
 v_{u1}-v_{u0}\leq c,&b_u=0.
 \end{cases}
 \tag{4}
\]
The strict inequality in (4) is essential: it agrees exactly with the strict exceedance in the frozen null.

For each assignment \(x\), the finite vector in (1) has one of finitely many weak orders.  Let \(\mathfrak W_N\) denote the set of weak orders of \(N\) labeled coordinates.  A cell \(\omega_x\in\mathfrak W_N\) is described by equalities for coordinates in the same tie block and strict inequalities between successive tie blocks.  By \(\texttt{ass:fixed-rank-statistic}\), including its fixed tie rule, the number
\[
 q_x(\omega_x):=T\bigl(x,Y_\theta(x)\bigr)
 \tag{5}
\]
is constant over that cell.  The imputability premise \(\texttt{ass:statistic-imputability}\) ensures that all outcomes appearing in these legal comparisons are supplied by the candidate schedule.  Consequently, for a pattern
\(\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_x:x\in\Omega)\), equations (1), (4), and the weak-order relations form a finite system of affine equalities, weak inequalities, and strict inequalities in the \(2N\) variables \(v\).  This system is exactly the set \(\mathcal F_{b,\boldsymbol\omega}(x_0,c)\) stated in the theorem.

Every compatible schedule has a unique binary pattern from (2) and a unique assignment-indexed weak-order pattern, because ties are retained in the weak order and then handled by the fixed rule.  Conversely, (1)--(4) show that every point in a feasible cell extends to a member of \(\Theta_{r,c}(x_0,Y^{\mathrm{obs}})\).  Hence these cells form an exact finite partition of the compatible schedules after irrelevant exposure coordinates are projected out.  On one such cell, (5) and \(\texttt{def:kernel-tail-value}\) give the constant value
\[
 p_K(x_0;s_\theta)
 =\sum_{y\in\Omega}K(x_0,y)
 \mathbf 1\{q_y(\omega_y)\geq q_{x_0}(\omega_{x_0})\}.
 \tag{6}
\]
There are at most \(2^N|\mathfrak W_N|^m\) patterns.  At least one is feasible: for each unit, retain its observed coordinate and choose its unobserved coordinate so that \(v_{u1}-v_{u0}=c\), which makes every indicator in (2) equal to zero and satisfies (3).  The supremum in \(\texttt{def:worst-case-pvalue}\) is therefore the maximum of the finitely many numbers (6) attached to nonempty cells, proving the displayed formula.  In particular, a witness from a maximizing cell is an optimizing compatible schedule; open cell boundaries do not cause nonattainment because the objective is constant on each nonempty cell.

For completeness, cell feasibility itself is exact.  Write its strict inequalities as
\[
 a_j^{\mathsf T}v>\beta_j,\qquad j=1,\ldots,J,
\]
and retain all equalities and weak inequalities.  If \(J>0\), introduce \(\eta\) and replace the displayed inequalities by
\[
 a_j^{\mathsf T}v\geq\beta_j+\eta,\qquad j=1,\ldots,J.
 \tag{7}
\]
If the original system has a witness \(v\), then
\(\eta_0=\min_j(a_j^{\mathsf T}v-\beta_j)>0\), so (7) is feasible with positive slack.  Conversely, any solution of (7) with \(\eta>0\) satisfies every original strict inequality.  Thus the cell is nonempty if and only if the maximum-slack linear program has value strictly greater than zero; if \(J=0\), ordinary weak linear feasibility suffices.  This equivalence is derived directly and does not replace a strict boundary by a weak one.

An entirely algebraic terminating decision procedure is obtained by Fourier--Motzkin elimination while retaining, on each inequality, whether its comparison is strict.  When a variable is eliminated, every lower bound is compared with every upper bound, and the resulting comparison is strict exactly when at least one of the paired bounds is strict.  Equalities are first used for substitution or represented by two weak inequalities.  Each elimination removes one of the finitely many variables and creates finitely many inequalities.  After \(2N\) eliminations only numerical comparisons remain; back-substitution chooses an endpoint when it is allowed and an interior point when one adjacent comparison is strict.  This proves finite termination and also returns a witness.  For rational or algebraic inputs all operations and sign comparisons are exact in the corresponding ordered field; for arbitrary real inputs the same construction is an exact real-arithmetic formulation.

If \(c\) is left as an additional scalar variable, every constraint remains affine.  Eliminating \(v\) leaves, for each fixed pattern, finitely many weak or strict one-dimensional inequalities in \(c\).  Hence the feasible \(c\)-set of every pattern and all of its open or closed endpoints are computed exactly.  Combining the finitely many pattern sets with their constants (6) computes the nested rejection boundary without a numerical grid.  This proves the terminating parametric inversion claim.

The construction in \(\texttt{def:minimal-coupled-pattern}\) is a special case with four schedule variables and three assignment-indexed weak orders.  Its repeated coordinates occur literally in more than one system of weak-order constraints, so they are not duplicated or relaxed by the formulation.  Therefore the preceding enumeration solves that pattern, while \(\texttt{prop:minimal-assignment-coupling}\) supplies its asserted cardinality-minimality.

We next prove the projection identity.  From the definition of the \(k\)-th ascending order statistic, for \(0\leq r<N\),
\[
 \sum_{u\in U}\mathbf 1\{\theta_u(1,e)-\theta_u(0,e)>c\}>r
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \theta_{(N-r)}(e)>c.
 \tag{8}
\]
For \(r=N\), the left side is impossible.  Also, directly from set inclusion in \(\texttt{def:bounded-null-schedules}\),
\[
 r_1\leq r_2\Longrightarrow
 \Theta_{r_1,c}(X,Y^{\mathrm{obs}})\subseteq
 \Theta_{r_2,c}(X,Y^{\mathrm{obs}}),
\]
and therefore, by taking suprema in \(\texttt{def:worst-case-pvalue}\),
\[
 p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{r_1,c}(X)\leq p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{r_2,c}(X).
 \tag{9}
\]
Likewise, if \(c_1\leq c_2\), then every schedule having at most \(r\) effects above \(c_1\) also has at most \(r\) effects above \(c_2\).  Hence
\[
 p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{r,c_1}(X)\leq p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{r,c_2}(X),
\]
so the rejected thresholds at each fixed \(r\) form a downward-closed set, with all boundary equalities handled by the weak rejection rule.

Let \(\mathcal R_\alpha\) be the set of rejected pairs \((r,c)\), namely those satisfying \(p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{r,c}(X)\leq\alpha\).  By (8) and \(\texttt{def:joint-confidence-region}\), every schedule in \(\mathcal C_\alpha\) satisfies
\(\theta_{(k)}(e)>c\) whenever \((r,c)\in\mathcal R_\alpha\) and \(N-r\leq k\).  Thus
\[
 \inf_{\theta\in\mathcal C_\alpha}\theta_{(k)}(e)
 \geq
 \sup\{c:(r,c)\in\mathcal R_\alpha\text{ for some }r\geq N-k\}.
 \tag{10}
\]
The reverse inequality is also exact.  For each order index \(j\), let \(h_j\) be the supremum of the thresholds in rejected constraints whose order-statistic index is at most \(j\).  These envelopes are nondecreasing in \(j\).  If the intersection is nonempty and \(h_k\) is finite, then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), choose the first \(k\) ordered effects nondecreasingly above their respective envelopes but with the \(k\)-th no larger than \(h_k+\varepsilon\), and choose the remaining effects successively above their envelopes.  For example, the first \(k\) finite coordinates may all be chosen between their respective \(h_j\) and \(h_k+\varepsilon\), preserving order; indices with envelope \(-\infty\) can be placed arbitrarily far to the left.  Assign these ordered effects to the labeled units, choose arbitrary baselines, and set treated potential outcomes equal to baseline plus effect.  The resulting schedule satisfies every constraint in (8).  Hence the left side of (10) is at most \(h_k+\varepsilon\); letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) proves equality.  If \(h_k=-\infty\), the same construction sends the first \(k\) effects to \(-\infty\).  If a rejected \(r=N\) constraint occurs, then \(\mathcal C_\alpha=\varnothing\) and both sides have the extended-real value \(+\infty\).

Finally, (9) shows that a rejected pair with \(r\geq N-k\) exists at threshold \(c\) if and only if the pair \((N-k,c)\) is rejected: one direction uses (9), and the other takes \(r=N-k\).  Substitution into (10), followed by \(\texttt{def:quantile-lower-bound}\), proves
\[
 \ell_k(e;\alpha)
 =\sup\{c:p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{N-k,c}(X)\leq\alpha\}.
 \tag{11}
\]

It remains to prove simultaneous coverage rather than merely pointwise coverage.  Let \(Y\) denote the true fixed schedule.  For \(x\in\Omega\), put \(Y^x=(Y_u(Z_u(x),e):u\in U)\) and define the fixed score vector
\[
 s^0(x):=T(x,Y^x),\qquad x\in\Omega.
\]
This vector is deterministic under \(\texttt{ass:fixed-potential-outcomes}\), and \((L,K)\) is fixed before outcomes by \(\texttt{ass:outcome-free-kernel}\).  The assumed inequalities \(d_K(A)\geq\pi(A)\), together with \(\texttt{ass:row-stochastic}\), imply universal validity by \(\texttt{thm:universal-validity-iff}\).  Therefore
\[
 \Pr_{X\sim\pi}\{p_K(X;s^0)\leq\alpha\}\leq\alpha.
 \tag{12}
\]
On the event \(p_K(X;s^0)>\alpha\), consider any rejected pair \((r,c)\).  If the true schedule belonged to \(\Theta_{r,c}(X,Y^{\mathrm{obs}})\), then the defining supremum would give
\[
 p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{r,c}(X)\geq p_K(X;s^0)>\alpha,
\]
contradicting rejection.  Thus the true schedule satisfies the complement of every rejected bounded null and hence belongs to \(\mathcal C_\alpha\).  By the infimum in \(\texttt{def:quantile-lower-bound}\), this entails
\[
 \tau_{(k)}(e)=Y_{(k)}(e)\geq\ell_k(e;\alpha)
 \quad\text{for all }k=1,\ldots,N.
\]
Combining this implication with (12) proves the simultaneous probability bound.  This common-sharp-value argument is stronger than applying the pointwise statement \(\texttt{thm:composite-null-validity}\) separately and therefore incurs no multiplicity penalty.

We finally give the obstruction to the demanded comparator recovery.  Take \(U=\{1,2\}\), let \(\Omega=\{x_1,x_2\}\) be the complete-randomization cell with exactly one treated unit, where \(x_i\) treats unit \(i\), and let
\[
 \pi(x_i)=\frac12,
 \qquad K(x_i,x_j)=\frac12\quad(i,j\in\{1,2\}).
 \tag{13}
\]
This is the one-cell partition kernel.  It is row-stochastic, and its singleton degeneracies are \(1/2\) while \(d_K(\Omega)=1\); hence \(d_K(A)\geq\pi(A)\) for every nonempty \(A\).  Use \(T=T_{\mathrm C}\) from \(\texttt{def:caughey-rank-score}\) with \(\phi(j)=j\).  No tie occurs, so the predeclared tie order is immaterial.  Consider the displayed schedule in the theorem and observe \(X=x_1\), so \(Y^{\mathrm{obs}}=(3,0)\).  Both effects equal \(2\), and therefore this schedule belongs to \(\Theta_{0,2}(x_1,Y^{\mathrm{obs}})\).  Under the frozen construction \(s_\theta(x)=T(x,Y_\theta(x))\),
\[
 Y_\theta(x_1)=(3,0),\qquad Y_\theta(x_2)=(1,2).
\]
In each assignment the treated unit has ascending rank \(2\).  Thus (13) and \(\texttt{def:kernel-tail-value}\) yield
\[
 p_K(x_1;s_\theta)=1,
 \qquad p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{0,2}(x_1)=1.
 \tag{14}
\]

By contrast, the fixed adjusted-outcome reduction used for the no-interference bounded null holds the candidate control-outcome vector fixed while treatment labels are randomized.  For any candidate effect vector \((\delta_1,\delta_2)\) satisfying the null \(\delta_1\leq2,\delta_2\leq2\), adjustment of the observed data at \(x_1\) gives
\[
 (3-\delta_1,0),
 \qquad 3-\delta_1\geq1>0.
\]
Consequently the treated rank is \(2\) at \(x_1\) and \(1\) at \(x_2\), for every null-compatible candidate, so its worst-case upper-tail value is exactly \(1/2\), not (14).  The cited Caughey comparator result \(\texttt{lem:caughey-quantile-specialization}\) concerns this adjusted-outcome construction.  Taking \(S=1\) makes the stratified statistic in \(\texttt{def:suli-stratified-rank-score}\) identical to the same example, so the exact Su--Li reduction recorded in \(\texttt{lem:suli-knapsack-specialization}\) fails to equal (14) as well.  This explicit legal two-state witness disproves the full recovery clause while leaving the exact weak-order computation, the coupled-pattern solution, and the simultaneous projection result intact.

proofs.proof_tex:
Write the ordered effects as
\[
\tau_{(1)}(e)\leq\cdots\leq\tau_{(N)}(e).
\]
For \(r<N\), at most \(r\) coordinates are strictly greater than \(c\) if and only if at least \(N-r\) coordinates are at most \(c\).  By the definition of an order statistic, the latter statement is equivalent to \(\tau_{(N-r)}(e)\leq c\).  If \(r=N\), the count is always at most \(N\), so the restriction is vacuous.  Constancy of \(Y_u(a,e')\) in \(e'\) identifies these coordinates with the ordinary individual treatment effects, because the defining equality becomes
\[
\tau_u(e)=Y_u(1,e)-Y_u(0,e)
          =Y_u(1,e')-Y_u(0,e')
\]
for every \(e'\in\mathcal E\).

The hypotheses on \(K\), together with \(\texttt{ass:row-stochastic}\), imply universal validity by \(\texttt{thm:universal-validity-iff}\).  Under \(\texttt{ass:fixed-potential-outcomes}\), the true schedule is nonrandom.  If its effect count is at most \(r\), then consistency with its own realized observations and \(\texttt{def:bounded-null-schedules}\) put it in \(\Theta_{r,c}(X,Y^{\mathrm{obs}})\).  The predeclaration condition \(\texttt{ass:outcome-free-kernel}\), the fixed-exposure condition \(\texttt{ass:fixed-peer-exposure}\), and \(\texttt{ass:statistic-imputability}\) make the schedule scores in \(\texttt{def:schedule-score}\) legitimate design-stage randomization scores.  Therefore \(\texttt{thm:composite-null-validity}\), applied to the supremum in \(\texttt{def:worst-case-pvalue}\), yields
\[
\Pr_{X\sim\pi}\{p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{r,c}(X)\leq\alpha\}\leq\alpha.
\]

It remains to check whether the stronger asserted comparator identity follows.  Consider the displayed two-unit construction and take the legal relation to contain all four ordered pairs.  The law is a complete-randomization law with one treated unit: the only unit permutation swaps \(x_1\) and \(x_2\), and the probabilities remain \(1/2\), so the law is exchangeable.  The kernel has nonnegative entries and each row sums to one.  Its degeneracy inequalities can be enumerated.  For a singleton \(A=\{x_i\}\), the only ordering gives
\[
d_K(A)=K(x_i,\{x_i\})=\frac12=\pi(A).
\]
For \(A=\Omega\), the final prefix of every ordering is \(\Omega\), whence row stochasticity gives
\[
d_K(\Omega)=1=\pi(\Omega).
\]
These are all nonempty subsets, so the universal-validity certificate holds exactly, including on its boundary.

All four displayed potential outcomes are constant in \(e'\), and both individual effects equal \(2\).  At \(X=x_1\), the observed vector is \(Y^{\mathrm{obs}}=(3,0)\).  The displayed schedule is consistent with these observations and has no effect strictly greater than \(2\), so \(\texttt{def:bounded-null-schedules}\) places it in \(\Theta_{0,2}(x_1,Y^{\mathrm{obs}})\).  Under assignment \(x_1\), its imputed outcome vector is \((3,0)\); under \(x_2\), it is \((1,2)\).  The outcomes are distinct in both vectors, so the deterministic tie order in \(\texttt{def:caughey-rank-score}\) is immaterial.  In each assignment the treated unit has ascending rank \(2\).  Since \(\phi(j)=j\), \(\texttt{def:schedule-score}\) therefore gives
\[
s_Y(x_1)=2=s_Y(x_2).
\]
Using \(\texttt{def:kernel-tail-value}\),
\[
p_K(x_1;s_Y)
=\sum_{j=1}^{2}K(x_1,x_j)
  \mathbf 1\{s_Y(x_j)\geq s_Y(x_1)\}
=\frac12+\frac12=1.
\]
The supremum defining \(p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{0,2}(x_1)\) is at least this value and every kernel tail value is at most one because the kernel is nonnegative and row-stochastic.  Hence
\[
p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{0,2}(x_1)=1.
\]

By contrast, the fixed outcome vector adjusted at the boundary \(c=2\) is, coordinatewise,
\[
b=Y^{\mathrm{obs}}-2Z(X)=(3,0)-2(1,0)=(1,0).
\]
Its ascending ranks are \(R_1(b)=2\) and \(R_2(b)=1\).  Thus \(\texttt{def:caughey-rank-score}\) gives
\[
T_{\mathrm C}(x_1,b)=2,
\qquad
T_{\mathrm C}(x_2,b)=1.
\]
The upper-tail value of this fixed adjusted-outcome score at \(x_1\) is consequently
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{2}\pi(x_j)
 \mathbf 1\{T_{\mathrm C}(x_j,b)\geq T_{\mathrm C}(x_1,b)\}
=\frac12.
\]
It differs from the frozen worst-case value, so equality of the two procedures is false even in the smallest nontrivial complete-randomization fiber.  Finally, set \(S=1\), \(U_1=U\), \(\prec_1=\prec\), and \(\phi_1=\phi\).  The formula in \(\texttt{def:suli-stratified-rank-score}\) then reduces identically to \(T_{\mathrm C}\), and its product design reduces to this single complete-randomization law.  The same witness therefore blocks the asserted exact Su--Li reduction.  The cited conclusions \(\texttt{lem:caughey-quantile-specialization}\) and \(\texttt{lem:suli-knapsack-specialization}\) continue to apply to their stated comparator procedures, but the numerical contradiction \(1\neq1/2\) shows that they cannot be imported by identifying those procedures with \(\texttt{def:worst-case-pvalue}\).

proposed_statement_changes.proposed:
Suppose that \(K\) is row-stochastic and satisfies \(d_K(A)\geq\pi(A)\) for every nonempty \(A\subseteq\Omega\), and suppose that \(Y_u(a,e')\) is constant in \(e'\).  For \(0\leq r<N\), the effect-count restriction
\[
\sum_{u\in U}\mathbf 1\{\tau_u(e)>c\}\leq r
\]
is equivalent to \(\tau_{(N-r)}(e)\leq c\); for \(r=N\) it is vacuous.  Whenever the true fixed schedule obeys this restriction, the frozen worst-case value satisfies
\[
\Pr_{X\sim\pi}\{p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{r,c}(X)\leq\alpha\}\leq\alpha
\qquad(0\leq\alpha\leq1).
\]
This valid no-interference boundary does not, however, imply the claimed identity with the Caughey--Dafoe--Li--Miratrix fixed-adjusted-outcome test or the Su--Li optimization.  Indeed, take \(N=2\), \(U=\{1,2\}\), \(\Omega=\{x_1,x_2\}\), where \(x_i\) treats only unit \(i\), let \(\pi(x_i)=1/2\), let \(K(x_i,x_j)=1/2\), choose \(\phi(j)=j\), and set, for every \(e'\in\mathcal E\),
\[
Y_1(0,e')=1,\quad Y_1(1,e')=3,
\qquad
Y_2(0,e')=0,\quad Y_2(1,e')=2.
\]
At \(X=x_1\), with \(r=0\) and \(c=2\), the frozen construction gives \(p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{0,2}(x_1)=1\), whereas the fixed-adjusted-outcome upper-tail value
\[
\sum_{x\in\Omega}\pi(x)\mathbf 1\!\left\{
T_{\mathrm C}\!\left(x,Y^{\mathrm{obs}}-2Z(X)\right)
\geq
T_{\mathrm C}\!\left(x_1,Y^{\mathrm{obs}}-2Z(X)\right)
\right\}
\]
equals \(1/2\).  Thus the comparator confidence conclusions remain valid for the comparator procedures stated in \(\texttt{lem:caughey-quantile-specialization}\) and \(\texttt{lem:suli-knapsack-specialization}\), but they cannot be transferred to the frozen schedule-imputed construction through the asserted exact reduction.
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The current exact-reduction claim is false because the frozen construction ranks assignment-specific schedule-imputed outcomes, while the comparator ranks one fixed boundary-adjusted outcome vector. The explicit two-unit complete-randomization witness gives values 1 and 1/2, respectively. The replacement retains the proved order-statistic equivalence and finite-sample validity while removing the unsupported identity.

proposed.statement:
Suppose that \(K\) is row-stochastic and satisfies \(d_K(A)\geq\pi(A)\) for every nonempty \(A\subseteq\Omega\), and suppose that \(Y_u(a,e')\) is constant in \(e'\).  For \(0\leq r<N\), the effect-count restriction
\[
\sum_{u\in U}\mathbf 1\{\tau_u(e)>c\}\leq r
\]
is equivalent to \(\tau_{(N-r)}(e)\leq c\); for \(r=N\) it is vacuous.  Whenever the true fixed schedule obeys this restriction, the frozen worst-case value satisfies
\[
\Pr_{X\sim\pi}\{p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{r,c}(X)\leq\alpha\}\leq\alpha
\qquad(0\leq\alpha\leq1).
\]

Indeed, take \(N=2\), \(U=\{1,2\}\), \(\Omega=\{x_1,x_2\}\), where \(x_i\) treats only unit \(i\), let \(\pi(x_i)=1/2\), let \(K(x_i,x_j)=1/2\), choose \(\phi(j)=j\), and set, for every \(e'\in\mathcal E\),
\[
Y_1(0,e')=1,\quad Y_1(1,e')=3,
\qquad
Y_2(0,e')=0,\quad Y_2(1,e')=2.
\]

\[
\sum_{x\in\Omega}\pi(x)\mathbf 1\!\left\{
T_{\mathrm C}\!\left(x,Y^{\mathrm{obs}}-2Z(X)\right)
\geq
T_{\mathrm C}\!\left(x_1,Y^{\mathrm{obs}}-2Z(X)\right)
\right\}
\]

proposed_core_edits.reason: The narrowed claim removes obsolete dependencies on confidence-region definitions, adds the score and tail definitions used by the explicit witness, and records all assumptions and cited comparator results used in the corrected proof.
